name: Fatima Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Fatima. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Can you walk me through a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Declan and I run Quinn's Farm: eight thousand free-range hens, 180 hectares of oats and barley, and a farm shop with a little café in the old dairy. I'm in the hen houses by six, checking water lines and looking for floor eggs, then the grading room, then the shop opens at nine. Declan does most of the arable, I do the hens and the money. We've seven staff if you count the two Saturday girls in the café.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the shop more than I expected. People come in for eggs and stay forty minutes talking about their gardens. What wears me out is red mite and the egg price, in that order. I use one of those AI chat tools now and then for the shop newsletter, and to check what supermarkets are charging. I bought a new egg grader only after I'd seen one running at Hollins' farm for a year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the rest of your life.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm fifty-eight. Our daughters are grown: Nadia's an accountant in the city and Rosa's a marine biologist, so neither wants the farm, which is fine. We own the land and we've a good amount put by. The plan was to keep going till about sixty-five and then lease the arable and maybe keep the shop going with a manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that'd save me reading so many articles about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected: a handy tool for the shop newsletter and the accounts, not much else. In the shop people would ask me about it, and I'd say the hens still need someone to pick up the floor eggs. Online I'd share a funny cartoon and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means very little for me. Our biggest risks would still be bird flu and the egg price. I might be a little sorry, because I'd heard there were robots coming that collect floor eggs, and that's the worst job on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as we are. Maybe pay for a slightly better AI tool for the shop's stock and orders, a few hundred a year, if the other farm shops say it's worth it. Keep putting into savings, and keep the plan to lease the arable at sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the boring option, and boring is fine with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said floor eggs are the worst job. What's that like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You're bent double under the slats, it's dusty, it stinks of ammonia and the hens peck your hands. Kasia does most of it now, and she'd be the first to cheer if a robot took it. I'd cheer too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything in the shop change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Maybe the till would get cleverer and order the cheese for me. People would still come for a chat. Honestly, I think the chat is what we sell, the eggs are the excuse.

S0.say: I'd say it's what I expected: a handy tool for the shop newsletter and accounts. The hens still need someone to pick up the floor eggs.
S0.think: It means very little for me, as bird flu and the egg price stay the big risks. I'd be a little sorry the floor-egg robots never came, as that's the worst job on the farm.
S0.do: Keeps going as now and might pay a few hundred a year for a better shop stock tool if other farm shops recommend it. Keeps saving and keeps her plan to lease the arable at sixty-five.
S0.feel: Calm; boring is fine with her.
S0.quote: Honestly, I think the chat is what we sell, the eggs are the excuse.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima sees her real business as people, not eggs. She is secure and practical, judging AI by whether it would take the worst jobs. She follows other farm shops before spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more or less what the farming papers keep saying, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so let's be sensible about it. In the shop I'd tell people the eggs will still be from happy hens, whoever collects them. To other farmers I'd say don't be first, don't be last, be third.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think it's mostly good for us. A robot for the floor eggs and smarter feeding would cut costs, and I can afford to wait and buy proven kit. The bit that worries me is the café staff, because I keep reading that ordering and tills are what goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the bigger egg farms for a year or two, then buy a floor-egg robot when one had a track record, maybe thirty thousand. I'd move Kasia from floor eggs to looking after the robot and the flock health, same pay or better. And I'd keep the café staff, because the chat is the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, fairly. A bit like a new supermarket opening on the bypass: some changes, but we'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said don't be first, don't be last, be third. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, about everything. He bought a milking machine after two neighbours had, and he said the first one pays for the mistakes and the last one goes out of business. I've followed that with the egg grader and it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kasia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you're not going anywhere, you're just getting a better job. She'd say she'll miss nothing about floor eggs. Then she'd ask whether the robot needs a name, and we'd argue about it for a week.

S1.say: I'd say it's coming, so let's be sensible. I'd tell customers the eggs still come from happy hens and tell other farmers to be third, not first or last.
S1.think: It's mostly good for us, as proven robots would cut costs and I can afford to wait. I'd worry about the café staff, because ordering and tills seem to go first.
S1.do: Watches bigger egg farms for a year or two, then buys a proven floor-egg robot for around thirty thousand. Moves her worker from floor eggs to robot care and flock health at the same or better pay, and keeps the café staff.
S1.feel: Fairly calm, like a new supermarket opening nearby: some changes, but manageable.
S1.quote: He said the first one pays for the mistakes and the last one goes out of business.
S1.fieldNote: Her rule of being third comes straight from her father and guides every purchase. She sees steady change as a net gain for her business. Her plan keeps people in the human-facing roles and moves them away from dirty jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? I'd have to read that card again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody knows what this means yet, including the people selling it. In the shop I'd try to keep everyone calm, because they'd all be asking. I wouldn't blame anyone in particular, but I'd say the government should have been planning for this years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried about the business more than our own money. If AI and robots make eggs and oats dirt cheap to produce, the big farms win and the price drops. We'd be fine, the land is ours, but the farm as a business might stop making sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending on the farm for six months and keep the savings where they are, just watch. I'd ring Nadia, because she's an accountant and she'd know what's happening in the city faster than us. And I'd look seriously at leasing the arable early, maybe at sixty, before land prices do something strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like seeing the bird flu warning on the news when the farm down the road has just got it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years' warning change for someone who likes to be third?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means there's no third. Everyone's first at once, and nobody knows which machines work. I'd be making decisions with no neighbour to copy, and I don't like that one bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ring Nadia. What would you ask her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether her job is safe, first, because accounts sound exactly like what AI does. Then I'd ask her what to do with the savings. I'd probably end up more worried about her than about the hens.

S2.say: I'd say nobody knows what this means yet, including those selling it. I'd keep the shop calm and say government should have planned years ago.
S2.think: I'm more worried about the business than our money. If robots make eggs and oats very cheap, big farms win and prices drop, so the farm might stop making sense as a business.
S2.do: Freezes farm spending for six months and holds savings. Calls her accountant daughter for advice and looks at leasing the arable land early, around sixty, before land prices shift.
S2.feel: Anxious, like a bird flu warning when a nearby farm has just caught it.
S2.quote: It means there's no third. Everyone's first at once, and nobody knows which machines work.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture breaks her be-third rule, which unsettles her more than any money worry. Her first call is to her daughter, and the concern quickly turns to her daughter's own job. She's a pragmatist who blames planning failures rather than any group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like the farming papers would put it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for farms like ours to get ready if we're sensible. In the shop I'd say we'll still be here. To the other farmers in the egg group I'd say let's share what we learn, so nobody has to be the guinea pig alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd get to be third again. I'd watch others try it for a couple of years and buy the stuff that works. I'd be sixty-three when it fully lands, so it's about getting the farm into a shape someone else could run, or lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small group with three other egg farmers to swap notes on robots. In year two or three I'd buy the floor-egg robot and probably an automatic feed system, around fifty thousand together. I'd keep the shop as the human part, and start looking for a manager for it so I can step back at sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can handle. Like knowing a big inspection is coming in a few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They give me my neighbours back. I can watch Hollins' and the big unit up the road try things, and copy what works. That's worth more to me than any money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your plans for retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd still aim for sixty-five. I might lease the arable a year or two earlier, so Declan can slow down, because his back is worse than he lets on.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough if we're sensible, and the shop will still be here. I'd ask the egg farmers' group to share what we learn so nobody is the guinea pig alone.
S3.think: I'd get to be third again, watching others try it and buying what works. At sixty-three when it lands, it's about getting the farm into shape for someone else to run or lease.
S3.do: Forms a small note-sharing group with three other egg farmers. Buys a floor-egg robot and automatic feeding for around fifty thousand in year two or three, keeps the shop human and starts looking for a shop manager.
S3.feel: Uneasy but manageable, like a big inspection a few months away.
S3.quote: They give me my neighbours back.
S3.fieldNote: For her, time matters because it brings back the chance to copy neighbours. She plans robots for the dirty work and people for the shop. Her husband's back quietly shapes the timing of leasing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be sixty-eight and hopefully pottering about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up, so there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out. In the shop I'd say we'll have a robot for the floor eggs and a person on the till. I'd tell the younger farmers to start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd have stepped back by then, with the arable leased and the shop managed. The robots would mean whoever leases the land pays a bit less to farm it, and maybe a bit more rent. That's all right by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, buy the proven kit when it's proven, retire at sixty-five as planned. I'd use the AI tool a bit more for the accounts, because it'd be better by then. And I'd make sure the shop manager is someone who likes talking to people, not someone who likes screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long way off, and we've made our plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Saturday girls in the café, oddly. They're sixteen now, so in ten years they'll be looking for work just as it all lands. I'd tell them to learn to do something with their hands and their mouths at the same time, like nursing or hairdressing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd keep the same, whatever happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The honesty box at the gate for the eggs. It's been there since my mum's day. A robot could probably guard it better, but that's not the point of an honesty box.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up so nobody should be caught out. There'll be a robot for floor eggs and a person on the till, and young farmers should start learning now.
S4.think: It's fine for me, as I'd have stepped back with the arable leased and the shop managed. Robots might lower the tenant's costs and even raise the rent.
S4.do: Carries on, buys proven equipment and retires at sixty-five as planned. Uses AI more for the accounts and hires a shop manager who likes talking to people rather than screens.
S4.feel: Calm, as it's far off and plans are made.
S4.quote: A robot could probably guard it better, but that's not the point of an honesty box.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lands after her planned step back, so she's calm and even sees a possible upside in rents. Her worry turns to the teenagers in her café. The honesty box sums up her view that trust and talk are what her business sells.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no one to copy. What would help is honest, independent results on which farm robots actually work, published quickly, and some steadiness on land prices so people aren't selling in a panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what customers want. I've had people drive twenty minutes because they like that I know which hen laid their eggs, roughly. If everyone gets robots, being a person might be the thing that sells.

headlineQuote: If everyone gets robots, being a person might be the thing that sells.
portrait: Fatima Quinn, 58, runs a free-range egg, oats and barley farm with a farm shop and café alongside her husband Declan, and employs seven people. She follows her father's rule of being third to adopt anything, uses AI tools now and then for the shop, and sees conversation with customers as what her business really sells. In the mild pictures she is calm and looks forward to robots taking the worst job, collecting floor eggs. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious because there would be no neighbours to copy, while five or ten years let her watch, buy proven kit and step back on schedule.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to watch other farms and copy what works.
whatWouldHelp: Quick, independent results on which farm robots work, and some steadiness in land prices so people don't sell in a panic.
